signal.title: Fix "Not-ready Set" for GLOBAL IN over an object-storage _path / _file filter
signal.text: `SELECT ... FROM s3(...) WHERE _path GLOBAL IN (SELECT ...)` over a path without globs threw ``` Logical error: 'Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument for function 'globalIn'' ``` `ReadFromObjectStorageStep::applyFilters` intentionally leaves the sets of `globalIn` / `globalNotIn` unbuilt, so that `ReadFromRemote` can attach an external table to them first. Plan optimization then moves the subquery plan of such a set into a `CreatingSetsStep` (`DelayedCreatingSetsStep::makePlansForSets`), which means the set is only created once the pipeline runs. `StorageObjectStorageSource::createFileIterator` prunes an explicit key list while the pipeline is being built, and its `buildSetsForDAG` call is a no-op for a set whose subquery plan is already gone, so the pruning expression was executed with a set that was not ready yet. `GlobIterator` is unaffected: it applies the same filter while listing objects, when the set is already built. Pruning the keys is an optimization - the same predicate is applied by the `Filter` step above the source - so skip it when a set is not ready. `buildSetsForDAG` now reports whether every set in the DAG ended up ready. Reproducer (deterministic, fails on `master`, passes with this change): ```sql SELECT * FROM s3(s3_conn, filename = 'x', format = CSV, structure = 'x UInt64') WHERE _path GLOBAL IN (SELECT 'no such path'); ``` The stress test hit it through an AST fuzzer query over `test_s3_race`: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=1c3181d592a4aaeec15077107e15b7edab5bca8d&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_release%29 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107619 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix the `Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument for function 'globalIn'` exception for a `GLOBAL IN` subquery over the `_path` or `_file` virtual column of an object storage table (`s3`, `azureBlobStorage`, ...) whose path has no globs.

signal.title: Fix set index on an expression with a Nullable operand
signal.text: A `SELECT` filtered on an expression that matches a `set` skip index raises `LOGICAL_ERROR`: ```sql CREATE TABLE events (id UInt32, INDEX b_set intDiv(id, 1000) TYPE set(100) GRANULARITY 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO events SELECT number FROM numbers(5000); SELECT count() FROM events WHERE intDiv(id, (SELECT 1000)) = 3; -- Code: 49. Unexpected return type from equals. Expected Nullable(UInt8). Got UInt8. ``` `SELECT 1000` is Nullable(UInt16), while the underlying column type of the index is plain UInt32, so when MergeTreeIndexConditionSet rewrites the predicate it loses the Nullable type and just saves that it is a UInt. However the equals function still expects a Nullable, and this mismatch throws an error in `ExpressionActions.cpp:executeAction`. ============================================ No `Nullable` appears anywhere in the schema or the query. A scalar subquery is typed `Nullable` because it may return no rows, and that is enough. In practice this shows up when the divisor or bucket size comes from a lookup or settings table instead of a literal; the typing is identical. Explicit wrappers reach the same failure: `nullIf(1000, 0)`, `toNullable(1000)`, `materialize(toNullable(1000))`. `MergeTreeIndexConditionSet` matched a query subexpression to an index key column by name only. Names are computed from constant-folded arguments and never include types, so `intDiv(id, (SELECT 1000))` renders exactly like the index expression `intDiv(id, 1000)` while carrying `Nullable(UInt32)`. The whole subtree was then replaced by the granule column while the enclosing `equals` was re-added with its already-resolved `IFunctionBase`, keeping the return type it was resolved with. `ExpressionActions::execute` binds inputs by name without checking types, so the granule supplied a non-`Nullable` column and the declared return type no longer matched what execution produced. `atomFromDAG` now binds the key column input to the type the granule block holds and restores the query-side type on top of it with `toNullable`, so the enclosing atom keeps the `IFunctionBase` it was resolved with. The atom function is not re-resolved from `FunctionFactory`, so there is no resolution failure to catch. A `chassert` pins the postcondition that the node handed back carries the type the query side expects. `toNullable` changes the type and not the data: the granule column's null map is all zeros, so `equals` produces no NULL, the `ifNull` that `traverseDAG` adds for a `Nullable` atom substitutes nothing, and the mask is bit-for-bit what the non-`Nullable` atom produces. Pruning is therefore unchanged rather than merely correct — `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` reports the same 5/50 granules for `t % nullIf(19, 0) = 16`, `t % toNullable(19) = 16`, `t % (SELECT 19) = 16` and `t % materialize(toNullable(19)) = 16` as for the plain `t % 19 = 16`. Two cases fall back to `UNKNOWN_FIELD`, which leaves the granule unpruned and sends the query through the regular filter path. A key column that is already an `INPUT` of the filter DAG, which cannot be re-typed, because a second input under the same name would be left unbound where `ExpressionActions::execute` maps each name to one block column. And a type difference that is not a `Nullable` the query side added: `toNullable` over the granule type has to reproduce the query-side type exactly, since dropping a `Nullable` the granule holds would substitute values for its NULLs. The regression test covers both granule filtering paths, since `secondary_indices_enable_bulk_filtering` selects between `getPossibleGranules` and `mayBeTrueOnGranule`, and each reaches the same actions independently. An index whose expression is itself `Nullable` is unaffected in either direction, because the types agree and nothing is re-typed; such an index prunes conservatively both before and after this change, because the granule genuinely stores NULLs and each maps to `UNKNOWN_FIELD`. Reproduces on the official release `26.8.1.727`. In builds with assertions enabled it aborts the server, which is how it surfaced in CI — 14 occurrences in 90 days across unrelated pull requests and every build configuration, through `tests/queries/0_stateless/01786_explain_merge_tree.sh` once the AST fuzzer wraps the modulus in a `Nullable` expression. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113234 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113233 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/89802 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111830 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `LOGICAL_ERROR` when reading a table with a `set` skip index defined on an expression and the query repeats that expression with a `Nullable` operand, for example `WHERE intDiv(id, (SELECT 1000)) = 3` over `INDEX b_set intDiv(id, 1000) TYPE set(100)`. A scalar subquery is enough to trigger it, since it is typed `Nullable`.

signal.title: Revert "Use libdeflate for gzip/zlib/deflate compression and decompression"
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114045 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108074 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Revert #108074 (use libdeflate for gzip/zlib/deflate): its streaming decompressor suspends only at DEFLATE block boundaries, so decompressing an HTTP request body whose single DEFLATE block spans the whole stream (the shape zlib-ng produces at level 1, which is the default in the official .NET SDK) was `O(n^2)` in the compressed block size and buffered the whole block in memory. A 22 MB gzip body that 26.6 ingested in 0.3 s took 15 s on 26.7. This returns the gzip/zlib/deflate paths to zlib-ng, restoring 26.6 behavior. The `gzip`/`deflate` compression levels `10-12` that 26.7 introduced stay accepted and are clamped to `9`, the maximum level supported by `zlib`, so configurations written against 26.7 keep working. ### Details This is a plain `git revert` of the merge commit of #108074, with the following manual adjustments: - `tests/queries/0_stateless/04230_iceberg_optimize_metadata_not_initialized_104711.sh` and `04240_iceberg_supports_parallel_insert_mv_104891.sh` keep their current (post-#108074) form: they now corrupt Iceberg metadata files directly instead of relying on `output_format_compression_level=11` being rejected, which works regardless of the compression backend. - The relocated doc `docs/reference/statements/select/into-outfile.mdx` documents the compression level range as `1-12` for `gzip`/`deflate` with the clamp, since the old `docs/en` tree no longer exists for the revert to apply to. The text for `http_zlib_compression_level` is changed in the `DECLARE` docstring in `src/Core/Settings.cpp`, because `docs/reference/settings/session-settings/http.mdx` is inside an `AUTOGENERATED` region and hand-editing it fails the `No direct edits to generated or read-only docs` check. **Backward compatibility.** 26.7 shipped `libdeflate` and, with it, `gzip`/`deflate` compression levels `10-12` on every output surface that routes through `CompressionMethod`: `INTO OUTFILE ... LEVEL`, `output_format_compression_level`, `http_zlib_compression_level` and the gRPC `output_compression_level`. A plain revert would narrow the accepted range back to `1-9`, so existing queries and settings profiles would start failing with `Invalid compression level` or `deflateInit2 failed: stream error`. To avoid that, `getCompressionLevelRange` keeps returning `1-12` for `gzip`/`zlib` and `createWriteCompressedWrapper` clamps levels above `9` to zlib's maximum. Levels above `12` are still rejected, as in 26.7. Two tests are restored in a backend-agnostic form instead of being deleted with the feature: - `04842_parquet_gzip_compression_level` round-trips a mixed-compressibility dataset through Parquet with `output_format_parquet_compression_method='gzip'` at levels `1, 3, 6, 9, 12`, keeping non-default-level coverage of `output_format_compression_level` for Parquet. - `04843_outfile_compression_level_range` covers the accepted `INTO OUTFILE ... LEVEL` range for `gzip`/`deflate`, the clamp of `10-12`, and the rejection of `13`. Additionally, gzip-compressed Parquet pages are now decompressed with a one-shot `inflate` loop (`decompressGzip` in `src/Processors/Formats/Impl/Parquet/Reader.cpp`) instead of the streaming `ZlibInflatingReadBuffer`. The streaming path could not tell a clean end of the gzip stream from a damaged one, because `zlib` validates the trailer (`CRC32` and `ISIZE`) only on the read after the one that filled the output exactly, while the reader stops as soon as it has `uncompressed_page_size` bytes — so a corrupted trailer was accepted silently. The one-shot loop requires `Z_STREAM_END`, while ignoring bytes left in the page after the last member, since `compressed_page_size` is the number of bytes the page owns and a writer may pad it. Two more tests cover this: - `04848_parquet_gzip_corrupted_trailer` corrupts a page's gzip `CRC32` in place and requires the read to be rejected, with and without page checksum verification. - `04892_parquet_gzip_padded_page` pads a gzip dictionary page and requires the file to keep reading back identically. A follow-up PR will re-introduce libdeflate with the streaming decompressor fixed to suspend at symbol granularity (linear time, bounded memory).

signal.title: Add `user_files_policy` server setting for custom disks in user_files directory
signal.text: Add a new `user_files_policy` server configuration parameter, similar to `tmp_policy`, that allows user files to reside on custom storage volumes, including S3-backed disks. When configured, the policy's volume (which must have exactly one volume) provides the disks for user file storage. All file operations (`file()` table function, `StorageFile`, dictionaries, `DatabaseFilesystem`, etc.) now route through the `IDisk` interface when a volume is configured, enabling S3 and other remote storage backends. Key changes: - `user_files_policy` setting in `ServerSettings` with XML config example - `Context` stores `VolumePtr` and exposes `getUserFilesVolume`, `getUserFilesPaths`, `setUserFilesPolicy` - `StorageFile` supports disk-based glob matching via `listFilesWithRegexpMatchingOnDisk`, disk-based reads via `disk->readFile`, and disk-based writes via `disk->writeFile` - `FunctionFile` reads through disk I/O when volume is configured - All 13 callers of `getUserFilesPath` updated for multi-path validation - Helper overloads `pathStartsWith(path, vector)` and `fileOrSymlinkPathStartsWith(path, vector)` added - Integration test with local multi-disk and S3 (`s3_plain`) scenarios ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add `user_files_policy` server setting to store `user_files` on a custom disk, including S3-backed disks. This allows customers to have a "scratch area" for files in ClickHouse Cloud, shared among all replicas. Note: keeping as a draft, because the code is not generalized enough. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Introduces a new storage-policy-backed path for `user_files` and rewires many read/write and path-validation code paths (including remote disks), which could affect file access semantics and security boundaries if edge cases are missed. > > **Overview** > Adds a new server setting `user_files_policy` that binds the `user_files` directory to a storage policy (enforced to *exactly one volume with one disk*) and stores the resolved `VolumePtr` in `Context`, with server startup applying it via `setUserFilesPolicy`. > > Updates user-files consumers to become disk-aware when a policy is configured: `file()`/`StorageFile` switch to `IDisk`-based globbing, reads, writes, schema inference and truncation (plus new helpers like `splitUserFilesAbsolutePath`, `userFilesPathExists`, and symlink-escape checks), while features that require local POSIX paths (`ATTACH ... FROM`, SQLite, `filesystem` table function, static HTTP `file://`, FileLog, several dictionary sources, error logger, etc.) now explicitly reject remote `user_files_policy` disks. > > Adds integration coverage for local-disk and `s3_plain` configurations, including globbing, absolute paths, traversal/symlink-escape hardening, write/append/truncate behavior, schema inference, and expected rejections (e.g. partitioned inserts under `user_files_policy`). > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 04b03ad8df769f756aa699f0eb7eb7fff624da1b. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signal.title: Deduplicate the final DISTINCT in parallel
signal.text: The final `DISTINCT` merged all of its input streams into one and deduplicated them on a single thread, so `SELECT DISTINCT` did not scale with `max_threads` while the equivalent `GROUP BY` did - aggregation parallelizes its merge over two-level hash tables, `DISTINCT` had nothing of the sort. This repartitions the input streams by the hash of the `DISTINCT` columns instead of merging them: equal values then land in the same stream, so every stream can be deduplicated on its own, and what is left to merge is already deduplicated. The repartitioning uses `scatterByPartition`, which `SortingStep` and `ShuffleSendStep` already use. Whether the order of the step's output is free to change is only known where the sorting properties are, so the decision is taken in `applyOrder`. The new setting `allow_parallel_distinct`, enabled by default, controls it. It is not applied when: - the input is already globally sorted, because then `DISTINCT` keeps the order of its input and the repartitioning would break it; - there is a `LIMIT`, because the transform stops early anyway and the single stream keeps `LIMIT` returning the first values of the input rather than an arbitrary subset; - the streams are already disjoint - `allow_distinct_partitions_independently` covers that case and skips the merge entirely. `max_rows_in_distinct` and `max_bytes_in_distinct` keep their global meaning: the streams hold disjoint parts of one `DISTINCT` set, so the transforms add up the sizes of their sets in a shared counter and check the limits against the total. Enforcing them in the single final transform instead would have disabled the optimization for everyone who sets them - including all of CI, where the test profile sets both to `10G`. Every input chunk is split across all partitions, so the number of partitions is capped rather than following `max_threads`. On `SELECT DISTINCT number FROM numbers_mt(4e7)` the total CPU time the scatter adds grows by 8% at 4 partitions, 20% at 16 and 96% at 96; without the cap that turned into a wall-clock regression at high `max_threads`. Wall clock, minimum of 3 runs, aarch64: | workload | `max_threads` | before | after | speedup | |---|---|---|---|---| | 20M distinct `UInt64`, `MergeTree` | 4 | 0.442 s | 0.205 s | 2.16x | | | 16 | 0.458 s | 0.148 s | 3.09x | | | 96 | 0.502 s | 0.165 s | 3.04x | | 40M distinct `UInt64`, `numbers_mt` | 4 | 0.965 s | 0.545 s | 1.77x | | | 16 | 0.929 s | 0.360 s | 2.58x | | | 96 | 0.886 s | 0.299 s | 2.96x | | 8M distinct `String`, `numbers_mt` | 4 | 0.515 s | 0.288 s | 1.79x | | | 16 | 0.517 s | 0.093 s | 5.56x | | | 96 | 0.518 s | 0.083 s | 6.24x | The measurements were taken on a busy machine, hence the minimum of several runs; the existing `distinct_in_order`, `distinct_high_cardinality` and `sorted_distinct` performance tests cover these shapes, so the performance comparison job is the authoritative check. `DISTINCT` without `ORDER BY` has no defined row order, and the repartitioning changes the order it happens to produce. Two existing tests relied on it: `04109_sort_propagation_apply_order` asserts that per-stream sortedness reaches `DISTINCT`, so it pins the setting off, and `00585_union_all_subquery_aggregation_column_removal` gets the explicit `ORDER BY` it was missing. Other tests that depend on the incidental order of a `DISTINCT` may surface in CI and should be fixed the same way. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114532 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/48988 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Evaluate the final `DISTINCT` on several threads by repartitioning its input by the hash of the `DISTINCT` columns, instead of merging everything into a single stream and deduplicating it on one thread. Up to 6x faster on high-cardinality `DISTINCT`. Controlled by the new setting `allow_parallel_distinct`, enabled by default. Note that this changes the order in which a `DISTINCT` without `ORDER BY` returns rows, which was never defined. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Do not let a post-run coverage diagnostic discard a finished test run's exit code
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `NightlyCoverage` shards exit 1 after every test has already passed. CIDB gets a pseudo-test row `clickhouse-test` / FAIL whose whole context is `clickhouse-test exited with code 1`, while the report shows the shard `OK` with `Failed: 0`. On master: 83 such rows in 30 days, 26 nights, all 8 shards, 6 of them on one nightly. Cause: `main()`'s post-run coverage block printed one diagnostic line built from two `FINAL` aggregates over `system.coverage_log`, the only two statements in that block outside a `try/except`. `clickhouse_execute` defaults to `timeout=30` and re-raises after 5 retries, and the aggregates sit at that cap: the job's own exporter runs the same aggregate over the same 23.4-25.4M rows in 20-29s. The `TimeoutError` propagates out of `main()`, so `sys.exit(exit_code.value)` never runs and Python exits 1 with every result already collected. That costs a red job for a non-failure, and an exit status that no longer separates a test failure from a teardown timeout. The statement is deleted rather than guarded because in this job it is a vestigial duplicate: `CoverageExporter.do()` re-runs the identical aggregate about 30s later, prints a strict superset of the numbers, and raises when the row count is zero. Nothing reads `cov_rows`/`cov_tests`. A local run drops the export stage, so it loses the line rather than seeing it duplicated. Validated locally: the extracted block exits 1 before the change and 0 after, with negative controls confirming the probe is specific to this timeout. Every remaining `clickhouse_execute` in the post-run block is now guarded (checked by AST). The pre-run block is untouched: it is meant to fail the run when coverage is broken. Two siblings are left alone: `coverage_indirect_calls` is redundant the same way but already guarded, and `reportCoverage` is unguarded but no CI job passes `--report-coverage`. CI report, shard 3/8 of the 2026-08-13 nightly: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=3da3cf323b91553960bdf55780a3b94e9deb5793&name_0=NightlyCoverage&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28amd_llvm_coverage_per_test%2C%20per_test_coverage%2C%203%2F8%29

signal.title: Add SHARED REGEXP path placement policy to JSON
signal.text: Adds `SHARED REGEXP 'pattern'` to `JSON` type declarations so matching root-relative flattened paths are always stored in shared data instead of competing for dedicated dynamic-path subcolumns. This is useful for high-cardinality path families whose promotion would displace more useful paths. Matching is partial by default, like `SKIP REGEXP`. Set the persisted `JSON` type parameter `shared_regexp_use_partial_match=0` to require full-string matching. Typed paths take precedence over `SHARED REGEXP`; `SKIP` and `SKIP REGEXP` continue to discard matching data. Rules are evaluated against the complete path from the original `JSON` root, including derived sub-objects. The rules are compiled once into an immutable `RE2` matcher, with bounded rule count and pattern sizes. A single rule uses direct `RE2` matching and multiple rules use `RE2::Set`. `JSON` columns without rules keep a null matcher, their existing binary type encoding, and their existing row-placement path. Metadata snapshots are copied lazily only when retained placement provenance actually changes a type. Placement provenance is stored in part column metadata and retained by default through horizontal and vertical merges, wide and compact mutations, column renames, lightweight-update patch materialization, and `Array`/`Nullable`/`Tuple`/`Map` wrappers. Removing a rule therefore does not unexpectedly promote already-shared paths during a later rewrite. Set the `MergeTree` table setting `allow_json_shared_data_paths_repromotion=1` to opt into reconsidering those paths. Policy-only metadata changes inside `Variant` are documented as unsupported. The `Native` binary type encoding uses `JSON` encoding version 1 only when a policy is present; ordinary `JSON` types remain byte-identical version 0. The canonical `JSON` documentation and `Native` format specification are updated accordingly. Testing includes 18 focused unit tests and 9 stateless scenarios covering syntax, partial/full matching, root-relative sub-objects, all supported wrappers, flattened `Native` and `RowBinary` paths, horizontal/vertical merges, compact/wide mutations, renames, statistics, and both lightweight-patch application paths. An 88.6 MB real Elasticsearch `indices_stats` document produced 143,555 flattened paths; all 143,290 paths targeted by `^indices[.]` remained in shared data and none became dynamic. signal.title: Fix division by zero in `ReadFromMergeTree` when `StorageMerge` truncates the number of streams
signal.text: The `AST fuzzer (amd_debug)` crashed the server with `Integer divide by zero` on ```sql SELECT id FROM merge(currentDatabase(), '^t$') ORDER BY id DESC SETTINGS max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio = 1073741824, max_threads = 4 ``` The planner computes `max_streams = max_threads * max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio = 2^32`, which passes the existing overflow check (it only rejects values that do not fit into `size_t`). `ReadFromMerge::createPlanForTable` then passed `UInt32(streams_num)` to `storage->read`, truncating `2^32` to `0`. The child `ReadFromMergeTree` divides by the requested number of streams in `spreadMarkRangesAmongStreamsWithOrder` (`(info.sum_marks - 1) / num_streams`), so debug and sanitizer builds crash with SIGFPE (release builds happen to eliminate the dead division, since its only use is in a loop that runs zero times). `IStorage::read` takes `size_t num_streams`, so the cast was a pointless leftover — this change removes it and adds a regression test that crashes debug builds without the fix. Additionally (per review), `StorageMerge` multiplied the requested number of streams by `max_streams_multiplier_for_merge_tables` (clamped to the number of selected tables) with unchecked `Float64` -> `size_t` casts, while the planner only bounds-checks `max_threads * max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio`. Both multiplications now go through a shared helper that throws `PARAMETER_OUT_OF_BOUND` (like the planner check) when the product does not fit into `size_t`, with a second regression test. Also (per review), `spreadMarkRangesAmongStreams` and `spreadMarkRangesAmongStreamsWithOrder` clamp an unnecessarily large number of streams down to the amount of data, but the check itself computed `num_streams * min_marks_for_concurrent_read`, which wraps around for huge stream counts. The clamp was then skipped and the ordered path went on to `split_parts_and_ranges.reserve(num_streams)`, throwing `std::length_error` in every build — reachable both directly on a `MergeTree` table and, now that the stream count is no longer truncated, through a `Merge` table. The comparison now uses a division, which is equivalent (`min_marks_for_concurrent_read` is always at least one) and cannot overflow, with a third regression test. Also (per review, and confirmed by the AST fuzzer on this PR), a streaming read (`FROM ... STREAM`) bypasses the `spreadMarkRanges*` helpers entirely: `groupPartitionsByStreams` created one `MergeTreeCommitOrderSequentialSource` per requested stream with no clamp, so a huge `max_threads * max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio` product threw `std::length_error` from `pipes.reserve` (or would exhaust memory for merely absurd values). Since a streaming read has no marks by which the stream count could be clamped, such values are now rejected with `PARAMETER_OUT_OF_BOUND`, with a fourth regression test. The cap is 65536: a source costs about 35 KB (measured on a sanitizer build: a single streaming read over a one-row table peaks at 669 MB / 1026 MB / 4030 MB of RSS for 1000 / 10000 / 100000 streams, over a 557 MB baseline), so the million that the limit on the number of threads in `MergeTreeReadPool` uses would still allocate tens of gigabytes before the query could fail, which is exactly what the check is there to prevent. The number of useful streaming sources is bounded by the number of cores, so 65536 leaves several orders of magnitude of headroom. Found by the AST fuzzer on an unrelated PR: [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113010&sha=59507af89c33f62942e855b50b3e66704cbcf2e9&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_debug%29) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113010 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a crash (arithmetic exception in debug and sanitizer builds) when reading from a `Merge` table with a very large `max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio`: the number of streams was truncated to 32 bits, so multiples of `2^32` became zero. Also, throw an exception instead of undefined behavior when the product of the number of streams and `max_streams_multiplier_for_merge_tables` exceeds the range of `size_t`, fix a `std::length_error` when reading a `MergeTree` table with a huge `max_streams_to_max_threads_ratio`, and reject huge stream counts on streaming reads (`FROM ... STREAM`) instead of trying to create a source per stream.

signal.title: Improve the performance of `MODIFY TTL`
signal.text: `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY TTL` currently rewrites every part of the table, which on a large table means reading and writing all of its data just to change when rows expire. Very often the new TTL is the old one shifted in time - the retention period is extended or shortened, e.g. `create_time + INTERVAL 300 DAY` becomes `create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY`. In that case every row's expiry time moves by the same constant number of seconds, so the parts do not have to be rewritten at all: it is enough to shift the expiry timestamps ClickHouse already stores per part. This pull request adds that fast path, and the result for the user is that such a `MODIFY TTL` completes almost instantly instead of taking minutes or hours: ```sql CREATE TABLE test_fast_ttl (`id` UInt32, `name` String, `create_time` DateTime) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id TTL create_time + toIntervalDay(300); INSERT INTO test_fast_ttl SELECT number, 'AAA', date_sub(day, 100, now()) from numbers(100000000); -- Before ALTER TABLE test_fast_ttl MODIFY TTL create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY; -- 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 25.564 sec. -- After ALTER TABLE test_fast_ttl MODIFY TTL create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY; -- 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 0.046 sec. ``` There is nothing to enable and no new syntax: the optimization is applied automatically inside the `MATERIALIZE TTL` mutation that `MODIFY TTL` already produces, and a plain `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` benefits from it as well. The observable result is exactly the same as before - the same rows expire and the parts end up with the same TTL bounds - only the work is avoided. Per part, the mutation now does one of the following: - the part is fully expired under the new TTL - it is replaced with an empty part; - no row of the part is expired yet - the part is cloned (its data files hardlinked) and only its stored TTL bounds are shifted; - otherwise - the part is rewritten exactly as before. The fast path is only taken when it is provably equivalent to the rewrite. It requires that the unconditional rows TTL (`TTL <expr>`) is the only TTL of the table, and that the old and the new TTL are the same date/time column shifted by constant fixed-length intervals, so that `new_ttl(row) - old_ttl(row)` is one constant for every row. Calendar `MONTH`/`YEAR` intervals, `DAY`/`WEEK` intervals in a time zone with daylight saving time, and row-dependent expressions are all rejected. The proof is redone for each part against the TTL expression (and time zone) that the part's stored timestamps were actually computed under, so a part that lags the table metadata, or was written by an older server, falls back to the regular rewrite rather than being shifted unsoundly. The same applies to the boundary cases of the stored timestamps themselves: a part containing a row whose TTL timestamp is exactly `1970-01-01 00:00:00` UTC (which ClickHouse treats as "no TTL"), a shift that would move some timestamp onto that value, and a part whose stored TTL is already fully expired (which the regular rewrite drops wholesale, even when the new TTL is longer) all take the regular rewrite. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY TTL` no longer rewrites the table's data when the new TTL is the old one shifted by a constant amount of time (the same date/time column plus fixed-length intervals), which is the common case of extending or shortening the retention period. Fully expired parts are replaced with empty ones and the rest are cloned with only their stored TTL metadata shifted, which makes such an `ALTER` nearly instant. Cases where the shift is not provably constant - calendar month/year intervals, day/week intervals in a time zone with daylight saving time, or row-dependent TTL expressions - fall back to the regular rewrite. `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` benefits from the same optimization. <!--- Directly edit documentation source files in the "docs" folder with the same pull-request as code changes or Add a user-readable short description of the changes that should be added to docs.clickhouse.com below. signal.title: PromQL: run the generated SQL with the analyzer on the HTTP API
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113772 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The Prometheus HTTP API endpoints `/api/v1/query` and `/api/v1/query_range` now evaluate a PromQL subquery shared by several plan steps once, as the `prometheusQuery` and `prometheusQueryRange` table functions already did. Previously a request made with `enable_analyzer = 0`, or by a user whose profile sets it, rescanned the shared subquery once per referencing step. ### Description Related: #113772, which marks a PromQL subquery referenced by more than one plan step `AS MATERIALIZED` so it is evaluated once. `AS MATERIALIZED` is honored by the analyzer only, and the two PromQL entry points disagreed about the analyzer. `StoragePrometheusQuery::readImpl` builds `InterpreterSelectQueryAnalyzer` directly, so the table functions always run the analyzer. `PrometheusHTTPProtocolAPI::executePromQLQuery` hands the generated SQL to `executeQuery()`, which honors the caller's `enable_analyzer`. With the analyzer off, the endpoints rescanned the shared subquery and the `enable_materialized_cte` default that #113772 added there had nothing to act on. Reachable two ways, both measured: as a URL parameter, since `isSettingLikeParameter` turns any non-reserved query parameter into a setting, and through the user profile, which is how the old-analyzer CI configuration reaches it. The fix forces `allow_experimental_analyzer` on the request context immediately before the single `executeQuery` call, so the HTTP path matches the table-function path. The generated SQL is machine-built for the analyzer, and the caller's `enable_analyzer` should not change the plan of SQL they did not write. No setting default changes and results are unchanged. Measured with `read_rows` from `system.query_log`, analyzer off via the profile: `last_over_time(a) or last_over_time(b)` read 880 rows before and 624 after, while `sum(last_over_time(a))`, which shares nothing, read 288 either way. Results are identical in both modes, so a results-based test would pass either way. `test_generated_sql_always_runs_with_analyzer` in `test_query_api.py` therefore asserts the two settings the generated query ran with, over both endpoints, with `enable_analyzer=0` on the request. The materialization itself is covered by `04816_promql_shared_subqueries_materialized`. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> The new test passes with the fix and fails without it on the assertion under test, reporting `'1\t1' != '0\t1'`: the first column is what the fix sets, the second shows the request reached the handler. 10 of 10 repeats pass with the fix, and the whole `test_query_api.py` file is green under the default, old-analyzer and distributed-plan integration flavours; on the unpatched binary the other 10 tests in the file still pass, so only the new assertion moves. The `system.query_log` read waits with `assert_eq_with_retry(retry_count=30, sleep_time=1)`: the response is flushed to the client before the `QueryFinish` row is queued, so a single flush can precede the row and leave it waiting for the background interval. Measured on this instance the row appears 0.23s after the flush in 12 of 12 requests, and the longer retry does not mask the defect, since the unpatched arm still fails on the assertion. An earlier revision of this PR carried a larger standalone test with a per-shape `read_rows` bound. It was replaced at review request. </details>

signal.title: Add early short-circuit evaluation for OR/AND in the analyzer to prevent unnecessary scalar subquery execution
signal.text: <!--- Disable AI PR formatting assistant: true --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add early short-circuit evaluation for logical OR/AND expressions in the new analyzer. When resolving OR/AND functions, if any argument is a decisive constant (truthy for OR, falsy for AND), the entire expression is replaced with the constant value before argument resolution, preventing scalar subqueries in non-decisive branches from being executed. Resolves #83017 ### Details This PR adds early short-circuit evaluation for logical OR/AND expressions in `QueryAnalyzer::resolveFunction()`. When resolving OR/AND functions, the analyzer now checks if any argument is a decisive constant: - For `OR`: if any argument is a truthy constant (1, true, "true"), replace the entire expression with 1 - For `AND`: if any argument is a falsy constant (0, false, "false"), replace the entire expression with 0 This optimization happens **before** argument resolution, preventing scalar subqueries in non-decisive branches from being executed at all. Resolves #83017

signal.title: Build Debian packages for the release builds only
signal.text: The `Stress test` was the only job installing the Debian packages of the debug, sanitizer and CFI builds, and it can take the plain `clickhouse` binary instead — that binary is built and uploaded for every build type anyway. Every other consumer of the packages (`Install packages`, `Compatibility check`, `Upgrade check`, the server Docker images and the release jobs) runs on a release build. So the release builds keep their packages, and nine of the eleven packaging steps go away, together with the `DESTDIR` install that copies the whole binary, and the upload and download of the resulting packages. The stress test now sets up the paths the packages own from the binary: `install_binary` in `stress_tests.lib` symlinks `/usr/bin/clickhouse*` at it, installs the default `config.xml` and `users.xml`, and unpacks the self-extracting archive up front — decompressing a sanitizer build under `clickhouse start` would eat into its wait for the pid file and race any concurrent `clickhouse local`. `install_packages` stays for the upgrade check, which installs an actual release. Symbolization is unaffected: `clickhouse_split_debug_symbols` leaves `programs/clickhouse` untouched and strips only the copy it installs, so the binary artifact carries its debug info even for a release build. For the sanitizer builds `clickhouse-common-static-dbg` was empty to begin with, since they do not set `SPLIT_DEBUG_SYMBOLS`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signal.title: Pin enable_parallel_replicas off for 00673_subquery_prepared_set_performance
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113575 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `00673_subquery_prepared_set_performance` fails `TOO_DEEP_RECURSION` in `Stateless tests (amd_tsan, parallel)` on its 21-deep nested subquery. Reported by @ alexey-milovidov on #113575, whose own randomized-settings minimization pinned the culprit to `enable_parallel_replicas 1` + `parallel_replicas_for_non_replicated_merge_tree 1`. Two facts compose. `tests/clickhouse-test:1772` is the only site that sets `enable_parallel_replicas`, and it is guarded by `automatic_parallel_replicas_mode == 2` (`:1769`, p=0.25), so the culprit pair appears only on mode-2 runs. And `STACK_SIZE_FREE_RATIO` is 20 under TSan versus 2 otherwise (`checkStackSize.cpp:150-157`), so the `maximum stack size: 8388608` in the message is the raw stack while the enforced ceiling is 419430 B. The overshoot is against that TSan-only 5% budget, not against 8 MB. This is a CI signal problem rather than a user-facing one. Measured server-side at the byte ceiling a non-TSan build has (while still paying TSan-inflated frames), nesting is stopped by `max_subquery_depth` (default 100) with `TOO_DEEP_SUBQUERIES` at depth 100, and the stack itself is fine to depth 250. The deepest reachable query is depth 99. CIDB shows one row matching this signature in 180 days and none on master. So this pins the one setting on the one test rather than changing planner recursion: ``` -- Random settings limits: enable_parallel_replicas=(0, 0) ``` I did not use `-- Tags: no-parallel-replicas`: the dedicated `ParallelReplicas` job is `amd_llvm_coverage` only (`job_configs.py:789`, `:795`), so it runs at ratio 2 and uses 8.6% of its ceiling. It cannot hit this limit, and the tag would skip the test there for no benefit. No SQL is changed and the test is not skipped anywhere. <details><summary>Validation</summary> CI-faithful TSan build (clang-22, `-DSANITIZE=thread`, Build ID `7d85b446...`). The enforced ceiling is the independent variable, calibrated with `ulimit -s 7000` into the window between the two arms' measured depth-21 usage (355408 < ceiling <= 362576), since CI's absolute byte count is not reproducible here (CI's frames measure ~18% wider on the same compiler). | arm | result | |---|---| | pre-fix, culprit pair forced at the client, unmodified file | 5/5 `Code: 306`, control 5/5 pass | | pre-fix, real runner, 50 randomized runs | 18 fail / 50; every failure `mode=2` + setting `1`, every pass mode-0 | | directive parses (runner's own parser, real file) | `{'enable_parallel_replicas': (0, 0)}` | | clamp changes the value (runner's own `apply_random_settings_limits`) | mode 2: `1` -> `0`; mode 0: absent both ways | | post-fix, mode 2 forced, value read back | `epr_pre=1 epr_post=0 prnr=1`, 3/3 pass (same harness pre-fix: 5/5 fail) | | negative control: corrupt the directive to `limitsX:` | unparsed, `epr_post=1`, 3/3 fail again | | post-fix, real runner, 50 randomized runs | 50/50 pass, 6-12 runs drew mode 2, zero `306` | | `--no-parallel-replicas` and `--no-random-settings` | run, not skipped | The negative control matters because an unparsed `Random settings limits:` line is just a comment, and because ~75% of runs draw mode 0 and pass regardless of the directive. </details>

signal.title: Reject truncated/incomplete AI text function responses
signal.text: The AI text functions (`aiGenerate`, `aiClassify`, `aiExtract`, `aiTranslate`) could silently return a truncated answer. When a provider stops early — most commonly by hitting the `max_tokens` limit — it reports this in the response, but the shared base class `FunctionBaseAI` never inspected the signal and returned whatever partial text came back. For example, `aiGenerate('Write three sentences about the ocean.', map(..., 'max_tokens', '5'))` returned the fragment `The ocean covers more than` with no error. This change normalizes each provider's native stop reason (OpenAI `finish_reason`, Anthropic `stop_reason`) into a canonical `FinishReason` enum, so the base class can make a single completeness decision without knowing the provider dialect: - `Truncated` (token/context limit) → throws `AI_PROVIDER_RESPONSE_TRUNCATED`. - `ContentFilter` (OpenAI `content_filter`, Anthropic `refusal`) and `ToolCall` → throws `AI_PROVIDER_RESPONSE_INCOMPLETE`. - `Complete` (natural end, or a caller stop sequence such as Anthropic `stop_sequence`) and `Unknown` (unrecognized reason) are accepted, so benign non-`stop` reasons are not misclassified as truncation. The rejection is thrown inside the existing per-row `try`, so it is non-retriable (retrying would hit the same limit) and honors `ai_function_throw_on_error`: with `1` the exception propagates; with `0` the row becomes the column default. `aiEmbed` is unaffected (embeddings have no finish reason). Integration tests in `test_ai_functions` cover truncation (throw + graceful), content-filter, an accepted unknown reason, and the Anthropic `stop_sequence` (must not throw) and `max_tokens` (must throw) cases. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): AI text functions (`aiGenerate`, `aiClassify`, `aiExtract`, `aiTranslate`) now reject truncated or otherwise incomplete provider responses (e.g. when the model hits the `max_tokens` limit) instead of silently returning partial output. Behavior follows the `ai_function_throw_on_error` setting.

signal.title: Add a Chinese tokenizer (jieba) for the tokens function and text indexes
signal.text: <!--- Disable AI PR formatting assistant: false --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a `chinese` tokenizer for the `tokens` function and `MergeTree` text indexes. It segments Chinese text into words using a dictionary and a Hidden Markov Model (the algorithm follows [jieba](https://github.com/fxsjy/jieba)), with `coarse_grained` (default) and `fine_grained` granularities. Continues #80174. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) ### Implementation notes - The tokenizer is a from-scratch C++ reimplementation following the fxsjy/jieba algorithm (dictionary-based maximum-probability segmentation with an HMM fallback). The embedded dictionary and HMM model are generated from a pinned [cppjieba](https://github.com/yanyiwu/cppjieba) commit (MIT) and verified by SHA-256; regenerator scripts are included. - The engine lives in a standalone repository, https://github.com/ClickHouse/jieba_cpp, consumed here as the `contrib/jieba_cpp` submodule with a `contrib/jieba_cpp-cmake` wrapper that builds it against ClickHouse's in-tree abseil/darts-clone/zstd. Built by default (`ENABLE_CHINESE_TOKENIZER`); the dictionary ships in little- and big-endian variants and is `#embed`-ed per host byte order, so it works on big-endian targets too. - `hasToken` now bypasses the text index for any non-`splitByNonAlpha` tokenizer (use `hasAnyTokens` / `hasAllTokens` for tokenizer-aware matching). This also fixes a pre-existing case where `hasToken` over `ngrams`/`array`/`splitByString`/`asciiCJK` indexes could return wrong rows.

signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108459 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Description Residual flakiness after #108459 (which fixed `test_shutdown_cancels_backup` and part of `test_long_disconnection_stops_backup`). `test_long_disconnection_stops_backup` still fails intermittently with: ``` AssertionError: assert ('UNKNOWN_TABLE' in [] or 'UNKNOWN_TABLE' in ['FAILED_TO_SYNC_BACKUP_OR_RESTORE', 'KEEPER_EXCEPTION', 'SOCKET_TIMEOUT', 'CANNOT_READ_ALL_DATA', 'NETWORK_ERROR', 'TABLE_IS_READ_ONLY', 'NO_REPLICA_HAS_PART']) ``` raised by `NoTrashChecker.__exit__` (test_cancel_backup.py:375), which asserts every error observed in `system.errors` during the scenario is in `expect_errors` or `allow_errors`. Under a long ZooKeeper disconnection a replica can briefly observe `UNKNOWN_TABLE` during backup teardown. This is a benign transient in the same error family as the entries already tolerated for this scenario, so the checker wrongly rejects it as unexpected. Fix: add `UNKNOWN_TABLE` to `allow_errors` for this scenario, mirroring how `NO_REPLICA_HAS_PART` was added to this same list in commit e55610d4100 (#96961). The meaningful assertions are unchanged: the `"Lost connection"` check, the `3 < elapsed < 45` timing bound, and the `BACKUP_FAILED` status check.

signal.title: Add `GROUP BY ... WITH CLUSTER <distance>` modifier
signal.text: Add a `WITH CLUSTER <distance>` modifier for `GROUP BY` that merges groups whose key values are within the given distance. The same primitive covers three metrics: absolute difference (1D numeric), Euclidean (2D tuple), Levenshtein edit distance (strings). ```sql -- 1D: sessionization on a numeric key SELECT user_id, min(event_time), max(event_time) FROM table GROUP BY user_id, event_time WITH CLUSTER 1800 -- 2D: geo-hotspots by Euclidean distance on a tuple key SELECT (lon, lat), count() FROM cell_towers GROUP BY (lon, lat) WITH CLUSTER 0.01 -- Strings: fuzzy dedup by Levenshtein distance SELECT alt_name, count() FROM geonames GROUP BY alt_name WITH CLUSTER 2 ``` **Concept.** `WITH CLUSTER d` is one declarative SQL primitive that merges groups whose cluster-key values are within distance `d`, with chained (transitive) semantics: `a` and `c` end up in the same cluster iff there is a chain `a, b, …, c` where each consecutive pair is within `d`. The metric is chosen by the cluster-key column type — numeric → absolute difference, tuple → Euclidean, string → Levenshtein. The standard SQL alternatives are different per metric (window functions for 1D, PostGIS for 2D, self-joins or `pg_trgm` for strings); this PR replaces them with one clause inside `GROUP BY`. **Implementation:** - **Parser:** `ASTGroupByElement` / `ParserGroupByElement`. - **Analyzer:** `GROUP_BY_ELEMENT` query tree node; cluster info (key index, dimensions, distance) on `QueryNode`. For 2D, dimensions are detected before `expandTuplesInList` flattens the tuple. - **Planner:** `ClusterKeyInfo` propagated through `AggregationAnalysisResult`; aggregation produces non-finalized states. - **Execution:** `ClusterMergingTransform` (wrapped in `ClusterMergingStep`) dispatches to `generate1D` / `generate2D` / `generateString` based on the cluster-key column type. **1D — bucket optimization:** values bucketed by `floor(value / distance)` in a hash map; same-bucket rows merge unconditionally, only boundaries need distance checks. O(N log N) → O(N + B log B). On 10M rows / 9.5M distinct keys: **~5x speedup**. **2D — grid + DSU:** grid with cell side `a = d / sqrt(2)` (cell diagonal = d). Phase A merges in-cell rows via `SipHash`. Phase B probes 12 forward offsets in 5x5 neighbourhood, AABB early-rejects, unites cells via DSU. Practically linear on sparse spatial data. **Strings — q-gram filter cascade:** length filter → 3-gram inverted index with the Ukkonen lower bound (`common_qgrams >= max(|a|, |b|) - q + 1 - q*d`) → bit-parallel `editDistance` → DSU. Naive `O(N^2)` fallback below `N = 10000` (cheaper than building the index). UTF-8 strings are treated as raw bytes; codepoint-aware Levenshtein and partition-aware q-gram indexing are tracked as follow-ups. **Real-data validation:** - `hits` (8M rows): 1D sessionization matches `lagInFrame + sum() OVER` byte-for-byte (1,560,719 sessions). - `cell_towers` (12.1M LTE): 2D clustering preserves point count, produces real hotspots (Tokyo 776K, Seoul 704K, NYC 572K). - NYC Taxi (3M, ~100m): identical 4523 clusters vs PostGIS `ST_ClusterDBSCAN`; **~284x faster** (1.93s vs 547s). - TPCx-BB SF10 `web_clickstreams` (83M): identical session count to window-function reference. - GeoNames (1.09M deduplicated alternate names; 30k / 100k / 300k random samples): global fuzzy dedup with `WITH CLUSTER 2` runs in 1.9s / 12s / 82s — **~12x faster than ClickHouse self-join with a length filter** (39s / 385s / 962s) and **~11x faster than PostgreSQL `pg_trgm` similarity > 0.7** (19s / 191s / 891s) at 300k. Self-join and `pg_trgm` scale near-quadratically; `WITH CLUSTER` stays close to linear. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry: `WITH CLUSTER <distance>` in `GROUP BY` merges groups whose key values are within the given distance, with chained (transitive) semantics. Supports numeric keys (1D, absolute difference), `(x, y)` tuple keys (2D, Euclidean distance), and `String` / `FixedString` keys (byte-level Levenshtein distance). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) ## Related issues Implements "Aggregation with approximate and spatial clustering (+ strings)" from Intern Tasks 2025/2026. Related to #87836

signal.title: Apply read in order with ORDER BY for plan-based parallel replicas
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114723 Plan-based parallel replicas (`parallel_replicas_plan_based`) splits the plan at the reading step into a `UNION` of a local read and a fragment shipped to the replicas. The split marker was lifted through `Expression`/`Filter`/`Aggregating`/`Union`/`Join`, but not through `SortingStep`, so for a plain `ORDER BY` the sort stayed on the initiator above the union and neither the local half nor the shipped fragment contained a `Sorting` above the read. `ReadFromMergeTree::requestReadingInOrder` was therefore never called on either side and both announced `CoordinationMode::Default`: results were correct, but the read-in-order optimization was lost compared to classic parallel replicas, which uses `ReadPoolParallelReplicasInOrder` for the same query. The split now lifts through `SortingStep` the same way it already does through `AggregatingStep`: a full sort is cloned into the fragment and the initiator keeps a `MergingSorted` sort above the union. Each side then re-derives read-in-order from the same sort description and they agree on `WithOrder` / `ReverseOrder` - `ReverseOrder` was not reachable under plan-based parallel replicas before. Since `SortingStep::serialize` drops the limit, a top-N is restated as an explicit `LimitStep` inside the fragment, as `tryMakeDistributedSorting` already does; it is skipped when an enclosing `LIMIT` has `alwaysReadTillEnd`, so `exact_rows_before_limit` stays exact. This also fixes a pre-existing failure on the same path: `tryOptimizeTopK` injects an internal `__topKFilter` function that is not registered in `FunctionFactory`. It was suppressed for `make_distributed_plan` but not for plan-based parallel replicas, so `SELECT ... ORDER BY <non-primary-key> LIMIT n` failed on the replica with `Unknown function __topKFilter`. A read that carries Top-K is now excluded from the shipped fragment (`mergeTreeReadCanBeShipped`), so such a query stays local and keeps its Top-K filtering instead of being distributed. Suppressing Top-K up front instead was rejected: enabling `parallel_replicas_plan_based` does not by itself mean the plan gets shipped, so that would silently lose Top-K for queries that end up running locally anyway. Verified locally against a three-replica cluster: `ReadType: InOrder` / `InReverseOrder` and `ReadPoolParallelReplicasInOrder` are reached, the coordinator logs `WithOrder` and `ReverseOrder`, and results stay identical to non-parallel execution for `ORDER BY` with `LIMIT`, deep `OFFSET`, filters, `WITH TIES`, `LIMIT BY`, `exact_rows_before_limit` and a full-sorting merge join. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Apply the read-in-order optimization to `ORDER BY` queries when `parallel_replicas_plan_based` is enabled: the sort is now shipped to the replicas and merged on the initiator, so each replica reads in the sorting key order. Also fixes `Unknown function __topKFilter` for `ORDER BY` on a non-primary-key column with this setting enabled.

signal.title: Add experimental Wallaby floating-point compression codec
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110613 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the experimental `Wallaby` lossless compression codec for `Float32` and `Float64` columns: it adaptively picks the cheapest of constant, decimal (Frame-of-Reference or zigzag-delta bit-packing, with PFOR-style patching and ULP-adjustment lanes), or XOR encoding per 1024-value block. Gated behind the `allow_experimental_codecs` setting. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) **Motivation.** This follows the evaluation of the `Chimp` codec proposal (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/66467) and of the newer floating-point compression literature: `ALP` (SIGMOD 2024), `Elf` (VLDB 2023), `Camel` (SIGMOD 2025), `Kangaroo` (SIGMOD 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3802076, in production in Alibaba Lindorm since 2024), and the independent evaluation "Beyond Compression" (PVLDB 18(11), 2025). No single family dominates: integerization (`ALP`) wins on decimal-mappable data and decompression speed; the XOR family wins on non-decimal and mixed-precision data; run-length collapse wins on repetitive IoT data. `Wallaby` picks per 1024-value block, and its delta-packing of integerized values exploits time-series smoothness that neither `ALP` (plain Frame-of-Reference) nor the XOR codecs use. **Patent note.** The mantissa-erasure preprocessing shared by `Elf`, `Elf+`, `SElf*` and `Kangaroo` (erasing low mantissa bits derived from the decimal-place count and exponent) is covered by patent US 12,289,120 B2 (Chongqing University, granted 2025-04-29), including the decompression side. `Wallaby` deliberately does not implement it. All building blocks used here are prior art or openly licensed: `Gorilla` XOR (2015), windowed references with an explicit index (Chimp128, VLDB 2022), integerization with FOR bit-packing (`ALP`, MIT-licensed reference, already in ClickHouse as the shared `FFOR` helper), and delta/zigzag/run-length encoding. The encoder-side reference search is three O(1) hash probes, not Kangaroo's LZ-history algorithm; the on-disk format is original. **Decimal-scale chooser.** The decimal scale (`alpha`, now signed) is chosen per vector by measurement, not by a fixed rule: candidates are generated from four sources (the scales of 32 sampled values, with the sample grown up to 256 exactly when a stronger pruning bound would pay for itself; the trailing-decimal-zero structure of the quantized reference, which enumerates scales at which subsets of the vector become exact; the minimal scales of exception values, which discovers a high-precision minority the sample missed; and the exact scales behind tolerant votes, for when a voted scale fails on the rest of the vector), each candidate is evaluated against the full vector, and the smallest measured payload wins. Exceptions are bounded only by a size-based budget — a candidate is abandoned exactly when its exceptions alone already make it larger than the best encoding known for this vector, or when the running width of its packed lanes provably cannot come in under it. Pruning uses only provable bounds (counted sampled failures and failure carry-over from wider scales — never width extrapolation, which can prune true winners), so the chooser never skips a scale that could win. The scale that won the previous vector is evaluated first, and homogeneous vectors stay at a single full pass. **Lane capping, ULP-adjustment lanes, signed scales** (added after reading the pcodec, `ALP`, and FastLanes internals). The packed lane width can be capped below the widest value, exiling outliers into the existing exception list — PFOR-style patching, chosen in closed form from a width histogram for Frame-of-Reference and by an exact chain walk for the delta lanes. Values that integerize only up to a small distance are absorbed by a second bit-packed lane set of zigzag ULP adjustments instead of 10-byte raw exceptions (the idea behind pcodec's `FloatMult`): decimals disturbed by lossy arithmetic — a `Float32` round trip, a unit conversion — no longer force the vector to XOR. The scale is signed as in `ALP`'s `(e, f)` factorization: a negative scale divides by a power of ten, so integers ending in decimal zeros (cents, millisecond timestamps holding whole seconds) pack their cofactors, including magnitudes beyond the `Int64` domain. The XOR window search additionally probes the previous value's lookback distance, which interleaved series keep hitting. Per vector, the candidates compete on the cheaper of the exception list and the adjustment lanes, and only the winner takes one capping pass. These mechanisms are what moved sensors `temperature` −7 %, sensors `pressure` −3 %, weather `tempMax` −2.7 %, and the synthetic `smooth gauge` −11 % against the previous revision of the tables below. **Synthetic benchmarks** (this machine, `clickhouse local`, 10M `Float64` values per dataset, `max_threads = 1`, compressed size after `OPTIMIZE FINAL`; insert is the best of 3 runs, `SELECT` is `sum(x)`, mean of 5 runs; `PCO` is the pcodec Rust crate linked as a codec by #110613, compiled into the same binary, at its default level 8; smallest size and fastest insert / select per row in bold — times are in seconds, lower is better; dataset-specific, not a general claim. Benchmarking the intermediate revision that contains only the provable-bound chooser rework attributes the cost: on the mgbench and sensors `temperature` columns that rework alone accounts for 60–80 % of the slowdown (`load_one` 0.81 → 1.74 s of the final 2.00 s), while on sensors `pressure` and hits `EventTime` the wider candidate space that the new mechanisms open dominates (1.43 → 2.49 s and 2.15 → 3.19 s). The trade was made knowingly: the size wins above come from the same revisions, and the encoder keeps a running lane-width floor that abandons hopeless scans mid-vector and a double-buffered winner so no scale is quantized twice. **Comparison with PCodec.** `PCO` is the strongest competitor overall. On ratio it is the smallest floating-point codec on 9 of the 11 columns, and the standalone `pco` CLI compressing each column as one chunk does better still (e.g. mgbench `load_one` 36.7 MB, weather `precipitation` 32.2 MB): per-64-KiB-block operation costs pcodec 20-45 % of its ratio, since every block re-learns its tANS tables and delta state. On compression speed the two are now roughly at parity — `Wallaby` up to 2x faster on the hits columns and weather `tempMax`, `PCO` up to 2x faster on the mgbench and sensor columns. On decompression `PCO` is 1.5–2.7x slower than `Wallaby` on the columns where a `Wallaby` decimal mode wins (sensors, weather `tempMax`, hits `EventTime`) and *faster* on the XOR-mode columns (mgbench, hits `UserID`) — the serial XOR bitstream is the slowest of `Wallaby`'s decode paths, while pcodec's decode cost is uniform. Against `ALP`, `Wallaby` is smaller on all 11 columns — dramatically so where `ALP`'s Frame-of-Reference degenerates (hits `UserID` 155 MB vs 684 MB, hits `ResolutionWidth` 47 MB vs 142 MB, weather `precipitation` 72 MB vs 132 MB). A correction to earlier revisions of this description: in-engine `PCO` was previously reported as 10-70x slower. That measurement came from a local build affected by a build-system bug that compiles all vendored Rust code with `opt-level = 0` unless `-DSANITIZE=` is passed explicitly (a `contrib/corrosion-cmake` condition mistakes `SANITIZE=OFF` for an enabled sanitizer; CI is unaffected because it always passes the flag). The numbers above are from a corrected build; a separate fix for the build system is being prepared. **Where `Wallaby` is not the winner.** On columns dominated by entropy redundancy rather than numeric structure — the three mgbench columns, weather `precipitation`, hits `ResolutionWidth`/`UserID` — plain `ZSTD` and/or `PCO` produce smaller data. Chaining helps exactly there, because the XOR/EQUAL residues are more entropy-codable than raw floats: | Column | `ZSTD(3)` | `ALP, ZSTD` | `Wallaby, ZSTD` | |---|---|---|---| | mgbench `load_one` | **44.5 MB** | 56.0 MB | 49.0 MB | | mgbench `cpu_user` | **32.0 MB** | 46.1 MB | 35.6 MB | | mgbench `mem_free` | 48.4 MB | 54.4 MB | **42.4 MB** | | sensors `temperature` | 74.4 MB | 58.2 MB | **54.2 MB** | | sensors `humidity` | 80.2 MB | 55.1 MB | **55.0 MB** | | sensors `pressure` | 99.1 MB | 97.8 MB | **90.1 MB** | | weather `tempMax` | 29.8 MB | 29.2 MB | **27.6 MB** | | weather `precipitation` | 56.4 MB | **54.6 MB** | 65.7 MB | | hits `EventTime` (F64) | 235.6 MB | **212.8 MB** | 213.0 MB | | hits `ResolutionWidth` | **37.9 MB** | 57.8 MB | 43.2 MB | | hits `UserID` (F64) | **149.7 MB** | 192.5 MB | 154.5 MB | `CODEC(Wallaby, ZSTD)` is the best of the three on 5 of the 11 columns — on the sensor columns and weather `tempMax` now by a clear margin where the previous revision tied `ALP, ZSTD` — and within 0.1 % on `EventTime`. The interesting exception is `precipitation`, where `ALP, ZSTD` wins because `ALP`'s plain Frame-of-Reference lanes on zero-dominated data are almost pure zero bytes, which `ZSTD` collapses better than `Wallaby`'s already-compact XOR runs. Side observation from benchmarking (independent of this PR): for `Nullable` columns the null-map substream appears to be stored uncompressed (+1 byte per row for every codec, including `LZ4`/`ZSTD`) — visible as a constant +22 MB / +31.2 MB across all codecs on the mgbench / sensors columns. Worth a separate look. Correctness: bit-exact round trip is verified by the encoder for every value with a per-value raw-exception fallback (`NaN` payloads, infinities, denormals, signed zeros, arbitrary bit patterns are all preserved; verified on random bit patterns and on all real datasets by multiset checksums in tests; the sensors dataset contributes 9298 genuine `NaN` values). The decoder validates all lengths and bounds, so corrupt input causes an exception, not undefined behavior; a decompression fuzzer target is included. An adversarial review of the current revision additionally round-tripped ~15M hostile values (per-block scale flips, `NaN` payloads, subnormals, domain edges) bit-exactly on both float widths. Note on the `NativeFormat` spec: the spec enumerates the column codec method bytes accepted on the `decompress=1` input path, so this PR adds the `0xa0` (`Wallaby`) entry with an experimental-status note, matching the existing `SZ3`/`Quantized`/`ZXC` entries. #### CI Settings (Only check the boxes if you know what you are doing): - [ ] Allow: All Required Checks - [ ] Allow: Stateless tests - [ ] Allow: Stateful tests - [ ] Allow: Integration Tests - [ ] Allow: Performance tests - [ ] Allow: All Builds - [ ] Allow: batch 1, 2 for multi-batch jobs - [ ] Allow: batch 3, 4, 5, 6 for multi-batch jobs --- - [ ] Exclude: Style check - [ ] Exclude: Fast test - [ ] Exclude: All with ASAN - [ ] Exclude: All with TSAN, MSAN, UBSAN, Coverage - [ ] Exclude: All with aarch64, release, debug --- - [ ] Do not test - [ ] Woolen Wolfdog - [ ] Upload binaries for special builds - [ ] Disable merge-commit - [ ] Disable CI cache

signal.title: Avoid copying data for the NONE compression codec when writing
signal.text: Avoid copying data for the `NONE` compression codec when writing. For `CODEC(NONE)` the compressed block on disk is byte-identical to the input, so the payload does not need to be copied between the compressor's working buffer and the output buffer. When a `CompressedWriteBuffer` exclusively owns its output buffer, the working buffer is now pointed directly into the output buffer (reserving room for the checksum and header in front of the data), so the caller writes the uncompressed data straight to where it will be flushed; `nextImpl` only fills in the header and checksum in place, with no payload copy. The header is written by a new `ICompressionCodec::writeHeader` helper factored out of `compress`. When the output buffer is too small, the writer falls back to the previous owned-buffer copy path. This is the same zero-copy buffer-aliasing technique that `HashingWriteBuffer` already uses. The zero-copy path (`out_buffer_is_exclusive`) is enabled only where the compressor is the sole, sequential writer of its output buffer: the wide-part column data streams, the primary-index stream, and the temporary-data buffer. It is intentionally left off where the output buffer is shared and written interleaved — the per-column streams of compact parts (which share one `plain_hashing`) and the network protocol buffer (interleaved with raw packet framing) — because there the reserved window could be overwritten by another writer. It is also left off for the marks streams of wide and compact parts: their `marks_file` has a small fixed-size buffer (4096 bytes), so the direct path would clamp `NONE`-coded mark blocks to it instead of the configured `marks_compress_block_size`; the regression test `04539_marks_compression_codec_none_block_size` covers this. Note: for `NONE`, compressed block sizes become bounded by the output buffer size, so the on-disk byte layout can differ slightly from before (an occasional shorter block at buffer boundaries). This is deterministic and does not affect reads. The read side already decompresses `NONE` data directly into the destination column via `readBig`, so no change is needed there. ### Performance evidence Measured with two `clickhouse` binaries built from the same base commit, differing only by this PR (cherry-picked onto the same parent), so the comparison isolates exactly this change. Isolated write-path microbenchmark — 4 GiB through a `CompressedWriteBuffer` with the `NONE` codec into a discarding sink (no disk), 1 MiB blocks and output buffer, toggling only `out_buffer_is_exclusive`: | `out_buffer_is_exclusive` | throughput | |---|---| | `false` (old copy path) | ~8.5–9.2 GB/s | | `true` (zero-copy path) | ~13.6–14.0 GB/s | | **speedup** | **~1.5–1.6x** | End-to-end `INSERT` of 8 wide `String CODEC(NONE)` columns (3M rows, single insert thread, no dedup/squashing/sparse, merges stopped; baseline = exact parent commit; median of interleaved reps): **2.96s → 2.62s (~1.13x, ~13% faster)**. The end-to-end gain is below the disk-free microbenchmark because disk I/O and data generation (equal in both binaries) dominate the rest of the insert. A focused performance test, `tests/performance/codec_none_read.xml`, is added. It scans `CODEC(NONE)` columns, so in the PR-vs-master comparison the table is filled by each side's own write path (old vs new block layout) and then read by the identical read code. This guards against a read regression from the slightly changed `NONE` block layout, and tracks `NONE` read throughput in general (relevant for incompressible data such as vector embeddings). Measured read time is unchanged before/after (~0.62s vs ~0.61s for 100M rows, single thread), confirming the write-path change is read-neutral. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Avoid an extra data copy when writing columns and temporary data compressed with the `NONE` codec by writing the data directly into the output buffer. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.title: Fix the bit-sliced full adder in `groupNumericIndexedVector`
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/106208 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110072 `addValue` set a bit when the computed sum bit was 1 but never cleared it when the sum bit was 0, so every carry left the lower bit set and the write path was not addition: ```sql SELECT numericIndexedVectorToMap(groupNumericIndexedVectorState(toUInt8(5), val)) FROM (SELECT arrayJoin([toInt64(10), toInt64(10)]) AS val); -- {5:30}, expected {5:20} SELECT numericIndexedVectorToMap(groupNumericIndexedVectorState(toUInt8(5), toInt64(1))) FROM numbers(8); -- {5:255}, expected {5:8} ``` Any repeated index whose addends share a set bit is affected, on every index type and in both the small and the promoted representation. `n` rows of value `1` at one index accumulate to `2^n - 1`. Additions whose bits are disjoint need no carry and were already correct (`10 + 5` gives `15`), which is why the existing tests and the documented examples — all of which use distinct indexes — did not catch it. Both writers are affected. `numericIndexedVectorBuild` replays every pair of its `Map` argument through the same path, and `Map` does not enforce unique keys, so a repeated key carries exactly like a repeated row: ```sql SELECT numericIndexedVectorToMap(numericIndexedVectorBuild(CAST(mapFromArrays([5, 5], [10, 10]), 'Map(UInt8, Int64)'))); -- {5:30}, expected {5:20} ``` `merge` and `numericIndexedVectorPointwiseAdd` share `pointwiseAddInplace`, which computes whole-bitmap XORs and assigns the result, so clearing is implicit there and those paths were already correct. That is why `numericIndexedVectorAllValueSum` disagreed with `sum(value)` over the same rows while merging the same values gave the right answer. `RoaringBitmapWithSmallSet` had no way to clear an element, so this adds a `remove`. `SmallSet` has no erase and the small set holds at most `small_set_size` elements, so that path rebuilds it without the removed value. `zero_indexes` is now maintained too. It holds the present indexes whose value is zero, so it has to gain an index when an update drives the value to zero and lose it when the value becomes non-zero — the same invariant the pointwise operations restore when they finish: ```cpp /// For any of the total_indexes, if it is not in the non-zero index of the result, the result is 0. total_indexes->rb_andnot(*getAllNonZeroIndex()); zero_indexes = total_indexes; ``` With that, adding `5` and then `-5` row by row produces `{5:0}`, matching what merging the two values already produced, and `numericIndexedVectorGetValue` and `numericIndexedVectorCardinality` agree with the map. The test asserts `numericIndexedVectorAllValueSum` equals `sum(value)` over repeated indexes with negative and fractional values, that the row-by-row path agrees with the pointwise path, that an index driven to zero is present with value zero, and that `numericIndexedVectorBuild` accumulates a repeated map key. Ten of its thirteen assertions fail without the fix; the three that pass are controls — an addition with disjoint bits, the pointwise reference path, and adding zero to an index that already holds a value. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `groupNumericIndexedVector` and `numericIndexedVectorBuild` producing wrong values when the same index is written more than once — several rows with the same index for the aggregate, or a repeated key in the map for the function. The bit-sliced adder never cleared a bit when the computed sum bit was zero, so every carry left the lower bit set: eight rows of value `1` at one index accumulated to `255` instead of `8`, and `10 + 10` produced `30` instead of `20`. Values that share no set bits were unaffected. An index whose value is driven to zero is now reported as present with value zero, consistent with `numericIndexedVectorPointwiseAdd` and with merging aggregate states.

signal.title: Add IPv4/IPv6 auto-inference for JSON shared data insertion
signal.text: Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/110761 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added `input_format_try_infer_ipv4` and `input_format_try_infer_ipv6` settings (both disabled by default) that allow ClickHouse to automatically infer `IPv4`/`IPv6` types from string fields during schema inference for text formats, following the same pattern as `input_format_try_infer_dates`. --- ## What does this PR do? Adds two new opt-in format settings that allow ClickHouse to automatically infer `IPv4`/`IPv6` types from string values during schema inference for text formats, following the same pattern as the existing `input_format_try_infer_dates` / `input_format_try_infer_datetimes` settings. ## New settings | Setting | Default | Description | |---|---|---| | `input_format_try_infer_ipv4` | `false` | Infer `IPv4` from strings matching IPv4 address format | | `input_format_try_infer_ipv6` | `false` | Infer `IPv6` from strings matching IPv6 address format | ## How it works In `insertIntoSharedData` (`JSONExtractTree.cpp`), after the existing Date/DateTime inference chain, two new blocks attempt to parse the string as IPv4/IPv6 using the already-existing `IPv4Node::tryParse` / `IPv6Node::tryParse` methods. On a match, the value is encoded with its native binary type (`BinaryTypeIndex::IPv4`/`IPv6`) instead of falling back to `String`. ## Storage benefit | Value | As String | As IPv4 | |---|---|---| | `"192.168.100.200"` | 15 bytes | 4 bytes | | `"10.0.0.1"` | 8 bytes | 4 bytes |
